title: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study
abstract: We report a preregistered, fully archived, verifier‑grounded comparison between a deterministic template baseline and a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version=gpt‑5‑mini) on 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks. A deterministic open validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) produced binary verifier pass/fail judgments on each generated configuration. Confirmatory paired analysis (N=120 pairs) found baseline success = 120/120 and gpt‑5‑mini guarded success = 120/120; paired difference = 0.00, 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729); McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Artifact provenance shows the confirmatory runs used preregistered generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (the same canonical candidate was supplied to both conditions per pair for seed_0). We therefore interpret the degenerate (perfect‑agreement) outcome as an artifact‑grounded fact about this preregistered pipeline and document why it does not imply operational equivalence. We release the full execution and analysis bundle (execution/*, analysis/*) and describe concrete next steps required to evaluate independent model generation under realistic NetOps diversity.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to convert operator intent into device configuration artifacts to accelerate NetOps workflows. Operational correctness requires more than fluent text: changes must preserve reachability, obey change‑ordering constraints, preserve BGP/ACL semantics, and avoid transient outages. Verifier‑grounded evaluation (using offline validators or emulators) is therefore essential to capture operationally salient semantic errors that token‑level metrics miss [1–3]. To provide reproducible, auditable evidence we preregistered CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1: a paired confirmatory study comparing (A) a deterministic template baseline and (B) an LLM single‑pass generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 programmatically synthesized intent→configuration tasks. The preregistration (SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) and the full execution artifacts are archived. The principal confirmatory question (H1) asked whether the LLM single‑pass success rate (verifier pass) is lower than the deterministic baseline (paired binary difference).
sections.related_work: Prior work explores LLMs for intent→configuration, verifier‑assisted generation, and configuration verification with tools such as Batfish and related control‑plane analyzers [1,2]. Recent studies argue for generate→validate→repair patterns and emphasize execution‑grounded validation to avoid semantic failures that are invisible to surface metrics [3–6]. Our study differs by (i) preregistering a paired confirmatory protocol, (ii) archiving every model call and validator trace, and (iii) reporting the artifact‑grounded reasons for the observed degenerate outcome.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study plan (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1) was frozen prior to execution and is included in the artifact bundle (preregistration SHA‑256: 7db1663c...). Key elements: task bank = 120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class: edge, datacenter, multi‑AS) programmatically synthesized and unit‑tested; conditions = baseline and guarded (gpt‑5‑mini single‑pass); primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; analysis = paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) and exact McNemar two‑sided test. Execution semantics and provenance (artifact evidence): the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) shows completed_episode_count = 240 and model_calls_used = 120. Critically, the preregistered generation_semantics for the confirmatory seed_0 runs was "shared_initial_candidate" (i.e., the same canonical candidate was supplied to both conditions per pair). Concrete artifact examples demonstrating this: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8becd7e1e36...), execution/responses/task-000002-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 ae967f70dfb6ccb8...). The validator records for the episodes are archived (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1ad...) and include validator_trace.final_state and validation status. Contamination detection: preregistered heuristics (exact‑match OR normalized 5‑gram overlap ≥ 0.95 flagged as 'suspected_contamination'; normalized Levenshtein ≥ 0.90 flagged as 'high_overlap'; self‑BLEU summary) were computed; the confirmatory set produced no flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv). Reproducibility: every prompt, response, validator trace, and seed is archived with SHA‑256 (execution/* and analysis/*; full hash manifest included).
sections.results: Execution summary: all confirmatory pairs completed (complete_pairs = 120), no infrastructure failures, model calls used = 120 (shared_initial generation stage per pair). Verifier outcomes (deterministic_netops_validator_v5): baseline successes = 120/120 (1.00); guarded (gpt‑5‑mini) successes = 120/120 (1.00). Paired contingency table: n_11 = 120, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, SHA‑256 9f25790c...). Estimated paired difference = 0.00. Bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 replicates, seed=1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.0. Representative archived episode (task‑000001): shared_initial candidate and both condition responses are identical (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 8f38c8be...); validator trace shows validation_after.valid = true and final_state fields matching the intended final configuration (see execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1ad...). Contamination check: analysis/contamination_summary.csv (SHA‑256 389227f0...) is empty for the confirmatory set.
sections.discussion: Artifact‑grounded interpretation. The observed perfect agreement (both conditions 120/120 pass) is a factual outcome of the preregistered pipeline and archived artifacts, but it does not establish operational equivalence between a deterministic template baseline and independent LLM generation in general. Three artifact‑backed facts explain why: (1) shared_initial candidate semantics — the confirmatory seed_0 runs used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate", so the same canonical candidate was supplied to both baseline and guarded for each pair (evidence: execution/responses/* shared-initial files, execution/execution_manifest.json); (2) validator–task coupling — the validator enforces the same intent/policy constraints used by the deterministic transformation pipeline to synthesize reference answers (transformation_manifest and task_manifest entries list the same required_sequence and constraint specifications), increasing the chance that template‑aligned candidates validate; (3) templated synthetic tasks — the task bank was programmatically synthesized from constrained templates with unit tests ensuring gold answers parse and verify, which reduces heterogeneity and favors template‑like solutions. Statistical consequence: zero discordant pairs render McNemar vacuous (p=1.0) and produce a degenerate bootstrap distribution concentrated at 0.00; this correctly reports the confirmatory evidence but cannot distinguish pipelines when they were supplied identical canonical candidates. Implications for NetOps evaluation: verifier‑grounded tests remain necessary, but confirmatory designs must ensure independence between conditions (no shared_initial coupling), include heterogeneous and adversarial task instances, and sample multiple independent generation seeds per task to quantify seed sensitivity. We archive all artifacts so others can re‑run alternative execution semantics (e.g., independent baseline generation or independent multi‑seed LLM sampling) without re‑creating the task bank.
sections.conclusion: Under the preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic confirmatory protocol (CAND‑2026‑001), both the deterministic template baseline and gpt‑5‑mini single‑pass generation produced verifier‑valid configurations on the N=120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks (both 120/120). The degenerate result stems from pipeline design choices that are explicit and artifact‑documented (shared_initial candidate semantics, validator–task coupling, and templated task bank) and therefore should not be generalized to unconstrained operational settings. We release the full execution and analysis artifacts and recommend that future verifier‑grounded NetOps evaluations adopt independent generation semantics, diverse/less‑templated tasks, multi‑seed sampling, and multiple validator modalities to assess real‑world reliability.

No human manually edited technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Confirmatory generation semantics and provenance (required revision addressed): the preregistered confirmatory runs used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate". The execution record shows that for each confirmatory pair the same canonical shared_initial candidate was supplied to both the baseline and guarded scoring episodes; representative artifacts demonstrating this are execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8becd7e1e36d8902e9ba2f09218baad021d77365b20...), execution/responses/task-000002-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 ae967f70dfb6ccb8b5dbcb1491775f30...), and the execution manifest execution/execution_manifest.json (completed_episode_count = 240, model_calls_used = 120). Consequently, the confirmatory paired comparison for seed_0 measures verifier outcomes on identical canonical candidates per pair rather than independent generator outputs; we state this explicitly in Abstract, Introduction, and Methods and document the exact artifact paths and SHA‑256 hashes above so readers can audit the provenance. Baseline derivation and reconciliation: the task manifest archives the deterministic reference answers produced by the task‑synthesis/transformation pipeline (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries and transformation_manifest.json). For the confirmatory seed_0 runs the baseline condition used the shared_initial candidate supplied at the execution stage (see execution/responses/* shared-initial files and hashes above). Contamination detection: preregistered string‑overlap heuristics were computed (exact‑match OR normalized 5‑gram overlap ≥ 0.95 flagged as 'suspected_contamination'; normalized Levenshtein ≥ 0.90 flagged as 'high_overlap'); no confirmatory items were flagged (analysis/contamination_summary.csv SHA‑256 389227f0d1e8...). Validator and scoring artifacts: every validator invocation and detailed validator_trace is archived under execution/scoring/ (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1ad..., execution/scoring/task-000002-guarded.json SHA‑256 993b8eb3...). Retry and failure policy: preregistered retry rules allowed up to two automatic retries for infrastructure failures; no such retries were necessary. Limitations acknowledged publicly: (1) shared_initial generation semantics reduce independence between conditions and must be considered when interpreting paired comparisons; (2) validator–task coupling and templated synthetic tasks limit external validity; (3) single canonical seed for confirmatory test limits assessment of seed sensitivity; (4) exact proof of absence of training‑data exposure is impossible though string‑overlap heuristics were run and archived. Full artifact release and reproducibility: the complete execution and analysis bundle (execution/*, analysis/*), the deterministic reconciliation report, and the full hash manifest are included in the submission package; paths and SHA‑256 hashes are recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json for audit.
limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: tasks were programmatically synthesized from deterministic templates and transformation rules; this favors regular solution forms and limits generality to heterogeneous operational intents.

Shared‑initial generation semantics in confirmatory runs: the preregistered generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair for seed_0; this reduces independent variability between conditions and must be considered when interpreting the paired comparison (see execution/responses/* shared‑initial files and execution/transformation_manifest.json).

Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary design used one canonical seed per task (seed_0) for the paired analysis; exploratory multi‑seed analyses were preregistered but are not part of the confirmatory result presented here.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces the same semantic constraints used to synthesize reference answers; this coupling increases the probability that both deterministic templates and generators closely matching the template grammar will pass, limiting construct validity for open operational distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: exact proof that the model was not exposed to template artifacts during pretraining cannot be provided; preregistered contamination heuristics (exact‑match, normalized 5‑gram overlap ≥ 0.95, normalized Levenshtein ≥ 0.90, and self‑BLEU) were computed and found no confirmatory flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv), but residual uncertainty remains.

Single‑model, single‑validator result: findings apply to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded execution conditions and validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); they do not generalize to other LLM families, multi‑step agentic pipelines, or different validators/emulators.
